title: The view from the top
hookLine: look back at five years: the stories, the practices, the texts, the questions, your own rule
tomorrow: why do the mountaintop stories end on the way down?

cards: At the top of anything, a trail, a graduation, a finished project, the phone comes out for the view. Petrarch, the Italian poet, climbed Mont Ventoux with his brother and wrote a letter about it.
At the summit he took in the clouds below, the far mountains, the distant sea. Then he opened the small copy of Augustine's Confessions he carried, at random.
On the page: people go out to admire the heights of mountains, the waves of the sea, the courses of the stars, "and pass themselves by."

teach.b: Petrarch wrote that he was stunned, and angry with himself for admiring earthly things. He closed the book and turned his eyes inward, and he says he hardly spoke on the way down.
That's Augustine's teaching: God and truth are found by turning inward, not only by looking out.

teach.h: GOD WITHIN, WHILE HE SEARCHED OUTSIDE.
teach.b: Augustine wrote that God was within him while he went searching outside. But notice what Petrarch did before he opened the book.
At the top, his letter says, he also looked back over his own years: how he had changed, and what he still struggled with. That's the view from the top, both directions.

teach.h: OUTWARD: HOW FAR THE TRAIL CAME.
teach.b: Outward: look how far the trail came, every switchback visible from here.
Inward: the slower view, how far you came. All the days on this path: stories told properly, practices, old texts, hard questions, and a rule of your own.
Augustine's line is a warning not to skip that second view. At the top, don't pass yourself by.

how: Augustine's Confessions are read for their turn inward toward God; Petrarch's letter about Mont Ventoux is read as a story of looking out and then within. People on this path look back at how far they've come, inside as well as out.

games.q: what does “the view from the top” mean?
o: the first moment you see a summit from below
a photo spot marked on a trail map near the top
looking back from the top at how far you've come

games.q: the view from the top: tap the pairs.
p: climbed Mont Ventoux with his brother

s: at the summit, Petrarch opened Augustine's Confessions at random
and found the line about people admiring mountains and passing themselves by.
Augustine's line praises climbing mountains for the view
it says people admire mountains, seas and stars, and pass themselves by.
at the top, Petrarch only looked out at the landscape
his letter says he also looked back over his own years and how he had changed.

games.q: your dad just retired and only talks about the projects he never finished. what would Petrarch's summit add?
o: look inward too: how far he came and who he became, not only what's undone.
nothing; looking back is vanity, so he should plan the next project.
he should stop thinking about himself and just admire the view.
games.why: at the top, Petrarch looked out, then looked back over his own years, and Augustine's line warned him not to pass himself by. the view from the top goes both ways.

practice: Stand at a window, or anywhere you can see a little distance. Look out first, as far as you can see, then let your eyes soften and take the inward view: one way you're different from when you began.

wordCard.voice: The view from the top: Petrarch's summit, and Augustine's warning not to pass yourself by on the way.

orig.note: Latin, Confessions 10.8: and they leave themselves behind; Pusey renders it 'and pass themselves by'.

carryVoice: The line to keep: look how far, out at the trail and in at the one who walked it. One day to the summit.

sources.ref: Augustine, Confessions 10.27 (God within, while he searched outside)
Petrarch, letter on the ascent of Mont Ventoux (Familiares 4.1)
